claims.text: In-situ tensile testing combined with DIC can capture the evolution of localized strain fields in FeNiCrMn HEA.
Localized strain maps can reveal the deformation mechanisms of FeNiCrMn HEA.
DIC can link microstructural features to the mechanical properties of FeNiCrMn HEA.
The proposed FeNiCrMn specimens have a uniform microstructure after homogenization, casting, or appropriate heat treatment.
DIC continuously records full-field strain during uniaxial tensile loading.
Controlled strain rates facilitate accurate DIC strain mapping.
Grain size, phase boundaries, and dislocation configurations mediate the deformation behavior of the alloy.
High-strain regions measured by DIC can be correlated with grain boundaries and dislocation pile-ups.
Microstructural features govern the yield strength of FeNiCrMn HEA.
Microstructural features govern the ductility of FeNiCrMn HEA.
Areas of strain localization will show a clear correlation with microstructural features.
The observed strain–microstructure correlation will help explain the alloy's strength and ductility.
Conventional tensile tests measure overall mechanical properties without mapping local strain variations.
Optical resolution limits DIC's ability to capture very fine-scale deformation.
DIC data may become less reliable at very high strain rates or for highly complex microstructures.
Surface-quality variability can introduce uncertainty into DIC measurements.
Post-deformation SEM can be used to examine microstructural changes in DIC-identified high-strain regions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis claims that DIC adds spatially resolved strain information to a tensile test, not that it changes the specimen's yield strength or ductility. The falsification rule nevertheless treats a lack of significant differentiation in global mechanical properties between DIC-enhanced and conventional tests as evidence against the method, even though those properties should ordinarily be comparable for equivalent specimens and loading.
